body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Five camp talks for Delphine, about how Delphine feels about the party and about the road. The talks that depend on how the party treats Delphine are not about any deed in particular. The companion is DELPHINE RAVELLE (call them Delphine in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these five talks, in this order, with these keys. Every talk is a private word at the fire in a different mood. Do not repeat a topic across them.

TALK strained. Delphine has lost faith in the party: the party's choices have drifted away from what Delphine holds dear (read the note's "Approval moments" for what they like and dislike). Do not claim a specific deed; speak of "the way things have gone" and name what Delphine cares about. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row (where they sit: apart from the fire, what their hands are doing), then 3 or 4 SAY rows saying what is wrong, in their own voice, stern and hurt, not shouting. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (listens, owns it, asks them to say what would mend it); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies: 1 reply row each for the cold one, 2 rows for the good one.

TALK doubt. Delphine is doubtful: not angry, but they have doubts about how the party goes about things. Gentler than strained, more puzzled and wary. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (takes the doubt seriously and asks what they would do differently); OPTION 2 answers coldly (a flip remark that brushes the doubt off); OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows for the other two, each with a REASON row.

TALK act1. The first night in Wickermoor, a few hours after the Ghostlight Express crashed. Delphine is still shaken and in their own way trying to be useful. They talk about the crash, the Hollow, the endless night and the Crooked Moon through their own eyes (their trade, their habits, their fears from the note), not about plot. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (a second NARRATOR row is allowed). Three options: OPTION 1 asks how they are holding up; OPTION 2 shares something of the party's own; OPTION 3 says they should get some rest and leaves it there. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act2. Deep in the troubles of the Hollow: the party has been through a lot and Delphine has seen the party fight, win and lose. Something small has shifted in how Delphine sees these people. Keep to the Hollow in general: name no place and no event except the Crooked House (the haunted manor on the hill, already cleansed) and the crash. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles as act1. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act3. The last stretch has begun; whatever is coming is close, and everyone knows it. Delphine is weary, truthful and a little funny about it, and says something about what the road has made of them and the party. Name no place and no event except the Hollow in general. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: strained, doubt, act1, act2, act3.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/delphine_ravelle-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for DELPHINE RAVELLE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Delphine likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/delphine_ravelle-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Delphine, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK strained
NARRATOR: Delphine sits on an overturned crate outside the firelight, snappin' her silver scissors shut against her thumb.
SAY: I signed on for a grand touring company, darling, not a pack of joyless bailiffs who treat every stitched soul like scrap for the bin.
SAY: You lecture the broken, you flinch when the spotlight gets hot, and you walk past every decent riddle with your boots loud on the boards.
SAY: If this is the way things have gone, I would rather watch my own seams rot in the rain than take second billing in a show without a heart.
OPTION 1: We have been wrong, tell us how to mend this.
OPTION 2: Keep your complaints to yourself and do your job.
OPTION 3: Stay by the fire and say nothing.
REPLY 1
SAY: Start by remembering that a creature made of spare parts still feels the shear, darling, and stop treating this valley like a ledger to balance.
SAY: Give me a little flair when the curtain rises tomorrow, and we will see if this frayed hem will hold another stitch.
REASON: You owned your mistakes and asked how to mend things.
REPLY 2
SAY: Spoken like a true taskmaster from the cheap seats, darling, so do not expect an encore when the house comes down.
REASON: You told me to keep my complaints to myself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Delphine slides the scissors into her coat lining and turns her button eye toward the dark trees.
SAY: Silence is a fine cue for an exit, darlings, so I will leave you to the ashes.

TALK doubt
NARRATOR: Delphine kneels near the edge of the embers, testin' the tension of a red thread between her gloved fingers.
SAY: I have been watching our little troupe work the house, darlings, and I cannot quite make sense of the choreography.
SAY: Half the time we charge through the curtain when a clever word would unpick the lock, and the rest of the time we play it terribly safe.
SAY: Mind the seams, darling, because a company that cannot decide whether it is a tragedy or a farce usually closes by midnight.
OPTION 1: You know the stage better, what would you change?
OPTION 2: Our way keeps us breathing, so leave it alone.
OPTION 3: Sit quietly and let the fire burn.
REPLY 1
SAY: A little misdirection before the blades come out, darling, and a willingness to take a bow when fortune offers a dare.
SAY: Let the monsters trip over their own hems while we read the fine print behind the scenes.
REASON: You asked how we could play our hand better.
REPLY 2
SAY: Breathing is a very low bar for a headliner, sweetheart, though I suppose even a wooden dummy manages to stay on the shelf.
REASON: You brushed off my doubts about how we work.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Delphine wraps the loose thread back around her wrist and smooths her velvet lapel.
SAY: Keep your cards against your chest if you must, darlings, the night is long enough for all of us.

TALK act1
NARRATOR: Delphine perches on a dry log close to the flames, brushing gray soot and pine needles from her hem.
SAY: Well, that was a dreadful way to make an entrance, darlings, tumbling out of the Ghostlight Express like spilled luggage.
SAY: Look at this sky, not a hint of morning in the wings, just that giant Crooked Moon grinning down like a sour critic in the gallery.
SAY: Back in Picco we knew how to string up proper lanterns, yet here in Wickermoor the fog smells of wet wool and old pennies.
NARRATOR: Above her left shoulder the empty air shivers once, as if something unseen just took a tumble.
SAY: Your Foolishness thinks the crash was a marvelous bit of slapstick, of course, because a floating head never has to scrub mud out of good felt.
SAY: He says you're lying, and he doesn't even have eyes, whenever I tell myself the next train will roll in by dawn.
SAY: Still, I refuse to let this damp hollow shrink my coat before we even find out who is running the show.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up after that wreck?
OPTION 2: None of us asked for this ticket either.
OPTION 3: Put the brush away and get some sleep.
REPLY 1
SAY: My pride took a nastier bruise than my stuffing, darling, though I did lose two perfectly good brass pins in the ditch.
SAY: Give me a dry fire and a decent audience, and I will be ready for the matinee by morning.
REASON: You asked how I was holding up after the crash.
REPLY 2
SAY: Then we are all booked into the same crooked theater, darlings, and we might as well steal the spotlight while we are here.
SAY: Stick close to my cue, and we will make sure the management regrets locking the doors.
REASON: You shared how it felt to be stranded here.
REPLY 3
SAY: A lady does not retire with cinder in her seams, darling, though I will rest my eyes once this velvet is respectable.
REASON: You told me to put the brush away and rest.

TALK act2
NARRATOR: Delphine sits cross-legged by the kettle, warming her palms near the steam while her glass button eye catches the orange glow.
SAY: When we first crawled out of that wreck, darlings, I figured you for a band of amateurs who would fold before the second act.
SAY: Ever since we walked out of that dreadful Crooked House with our skins intact, I have had to revise my review.
SAY: We have taken some ugly tumbles in this hollow, the kind where the music stops and the sawdust tastes like iron.
SAY: Yet every time the dark tries to pull our threads, somebody in this circle steps up and holds the line.
SAY: Even Your Foolishness has stopped placing bets on which one of you will bolt for the exits first.
SAY: In Funtopia, performers only caught you if the ringmistress was watching, and they always sent a bill for the trouble.
SAY: It is a strange thing, darlings, learning to trust a net you did not have to stitch yourself.
OPTION 1: How is that change sitting with you tonight?
OPTION 2: We watch your back because you are one of us.
OPTION 3: Save your strength for tomorrow and get some rest.
REPLY 1
SAY: It makes my chest feel a bit too tight for the buttons, darling, if you want the honest truth.
SAY: Still, it beats standing under the arch alone waiting for the rope to fray.
REASON: You asked how trusting the troupe sat with me.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Delphine tilts her chin up, tap-tappin' one booted heel against a root to hide the pause.
SAY: Careful with that sentimental billing, darling, or people will think I have gone soft in the felt.
SAY: All the same, if anything reaches for your collar out there, my shears are already open.
REASON: You told me I was one of your own.
REPLY 3
SAY: Very sensible, darling, the road ahead is bound to be muddy and I need my voice in working order.
REASON: You told me to save my strength and rest.

TALK act3
NARRATOR: Delphine rests her back against a pack by the low fire, her fingers still in her lap and her coat mended with three colors of thread.
SAY: Look at the lot of us, darlings, patched up like a carnival tent after a gale and still waiting for the final bell.
SAY: If Master Orsino could see this coat now, he would weep into his worktable over the mismatched stitching.
SAY: I spent my whole life terrified of coming unpicked, certain that one loose loop meant the end of Delphine Ravelle.
SAY: Now the biggest curtain in the valley is about to drop on our heads, and my hands are not even shaking.
SAY: The Hollow has chewed on our hems and spat us out, yet here we sit by the coals like we own the lease.
SAY: Whatever waits for us down that last stretch of road, it will not find a box of spare stuffing.
SAY: It is going to find a headliner and the finest company she ever shared a bill with.
OPTION 1: Are you ready for whatever waits at the end?
OPTION 2: Whatever comes next, we face that curtain together.
OPTION 3: Get some rest while the fire is still warm.
REPLY 1
SAY: I have my needles sharp and my lines by heart, darling, though I will admit the quiet before the cue is always the hardest part.
SAY: Keep the footlights burning a little longer, and I will give them a finale they cannot forget.
REASON: You asked if I was ready for the end.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Delphine reaches out and touches the edge of your sleeve with two gloved fingers.
SAY: Together, darling, right on the bias, and let the house lights try to keep up with us.
SAY: Win or lose, there is no other troupe I would rather take the last bow beside.
REASON: You promised we would face the final curtain together.
REPLY 3
SAY: I will close my eyes for an hour, darlings, so wake me before the overture starts.
REASON: You told me to rest while the fire stayed warm.
